title: Regulation of hepatic glucose metabolism in health and disease
authors: Petersen MC, Vatner DF, Shulman GI

result: Narrative review. Glucagon receptor (GCGR) activation raises cAMP and activates PKA, which inhibits L-type pyruvate kinase, phosphorylates PFK-2/FBPase-2 to favour its phosphatase activity and lower fructose 2,6-bisphosphate, an allosteric inhibitor of FBPase-1 (printed as fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase 1), phosphorylates and inactivates glycogen synthase, and activates phosphorylase kinase, which phosphorylates glycogen phosphorylase at Ser15; PKA also activates the CREB-CBP-CRTC2 complex for gluconeogenic gene transcription. FOXO proteins with PGC1-alpha raise PCK1 and G6PC expression and are excluded from the nucleus after AKT phosphorylation. Glucose enters hepatocytes by facilitated diffusion through GLUT2; glucose allosterically inhibits glycogen phosphorylase; glucose 6-phosphate is the key allosteric activator of GYS2. In overnight-fasted humans under somatostatin, hyperinsulinaemia was required to stimulate hepatic glycogen synthesis and hyperglycaemia to suppress glycogenolysis. Hepatic glucose production and storage are dysregulated in type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus, and this imbalance contributes to hyperglycaemia in the fasted and postprandial states. Metformin is used as first-line therapy for type 2 diabetes and acts primarily through the suppression of hepatic gluconeogenesis, by a molecular mechanism that remains under investigation. Several lines of evidence cast doubt on the necessity of AMPK: metformin continues to inhibit glucose production in Ampk-knockout primary mouse hepatocytes and improves glucose tolerance in Ampk-knockout mice to a similar extent as in wild-type mice. Inhibition of mitochondrial complex I is observed only at suprapharmacological, millimolar concentrations, in contrast to the clinically relevant plasma concentration range of 50 to 100 µM in patients who take 2 g of metformin daily. Metformin non-competitively inhibits mitochondrial glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase in isolated hepatocytes with a clinically relevant Ki of about 50 µM, which predicts impaired gluconeogenesis only from the redox-dependent substrates lactate and glycerol and not from pyruvate, alanine or dihydroxyacetone phosphate; the importance of the glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle in gluconeogenesis in the human liver is unclear, so studies in humans are required.
